candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Evolution proceeds through cumulative selection across immense spans of time, so a sudden random arrangement analogy misrepresents it.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted rebuttal is delivered by Silverman during his response to Turek's earlier Cheerios analogy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It directly contests the analogy used to make natural processes appear incapable of producing organized biological complexity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's Cheerios analogy portraying naturalistic development as a random spill suddenly forming an organized message.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman distinguishes gradual evolutionary accumulation from an instantaneous explosion or random spill and substitutes repeated incremental retention over time.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Biblical approval of violence against infants undermines the claim that scripture supplies objective morality matching ordinary moral judgment.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman explicitly introduces Turek's objective-morality claim and answers it with a biblical counterexample.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move attacks a principal theistic explanation of moral knowledge by alleging conflict between scripture and shared moral judgment.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's contention that objective morality exists and that torturing babies is self-evidently objectively wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman invokes a passage praising the destruction of infants and argues that the Bible can conflict with the moral intuition Turek treats as objective.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Morality is historically and socially relative, and accepting that fact places responsibility for moral choices on human decision-makers.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman develops the position continuously through the close of his speaking segment before the format transition.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It supplies atheism's affirmative account of morality and responsibility while challenging the practical value of purported divine objectivity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's argument that relativism cannot condemn atrocities and that objective moral duties require a transcendent standard.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman accepts difficult consequences of moral disagreement, argues that religious certainty can displace personal responsibility, and illustrates the alleged harm through historical and contemporary examples.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Relative morality still permits individuals and societies to object, judge, and assume responsibility without appealing to an external sacred standard.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman directly answers Turek's cross-examination question in a clearly attributable alternating exchange.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The answer addresses the immediate internal-consistency challenge that moral relativism would eliminate meaningful moral objection or judgment.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's challenge that Silverman cannot call an adoption decision immoral after denying objective morality.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman clarifies that denying objective morality does not end moral choice or protest; people still make judgments independently of holy books.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: An omnipotent, omniscient, and benevolent God should not require infants to suffer cancer, creating a direct problem of evil for Christianity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman deliberately changes the cross-examination topic to evil and formulates the challenge in his own extended questioning.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly tests whether theism better explains severe apparently unnecessary suffering under its central claims about God's attributes.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's claim that objective evil points to objective good and thereby supports the existence of God.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman denies that invoking objective evil resolves the issue and asks why a God able to prevent every case knowingly permits childhood cancer.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: Divine foreknowledge and deliberate placement of the forbidden tree make God responsible for the fall and its foreseeable consequences.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman presents the Garden of Eden scenario directly after Turek's free-will defense of the existence of evil.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It challenges the free-will defense by relocating causal and moral responsibility from human agents to an omniscient creator's prior decision.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's defense that evil entered the world through human free choice and that freedom is necessary for love.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman argues that God knew exactly what Adam would do and could have placed or omitted the tree differently, yet chose the foreknown outcome.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Although a sinless free world is logically conceivable, it may not be achievable because free creatures might sin in every feasible world.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek explicitly takes the floor to identify the assumption in Silverman's scenario and delivers the full response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal answer to the claim that God could simply create free agents while guaranteeing that no one ever sins.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's claim that God could locate or omit the forbidden tree so that Adam would not sin and suffering would not follow.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek distinguishes logical possibility from actual achievability with free creatures, then frames the resulting biblical story as redemption after freely chosen sin.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Knowing a future action does not cause it, just as knowing a recorded game's result does not remove the players' freedom when they acted.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek introduces and develops the recorded-football-game analogy in direct response to Silverman's foreknowledge objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy supports the crucial distinction between divine foreknowledge and divine causation on which Turek's free-will defense depends.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's argument that perfect divine foreknowledge leaves Adam no choice and makes God responsible for the fall.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek compares God's knowledge to a viewer who already knows a recorded game's score but did not thereby cause the players' original decisions.

candidates.speaker: Frank Turek
candidates.proposition: Finite observers cannot establish that suffering is gratuitous because its good consequences may emerge later, through other choices, or in eternity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Turek explicitly turns back to Silverman's gratuitous-evil challenge and gives a sustained multi-part response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly defends theism's explanatory adequacy against apparently pointless evil and connects suffering to limited human perspective and eternal justice.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Silverman's contention that childhood cancer and other suffering lack sufficient purpose and therefore make a benevolent God culpable.

candidates.contextSummary: Turek argues that humans cannot trace all causal consequences, uses ripple effects to illustrate unknown goods, and adds that divine justice extends beyond earthly life.

candidates.speaker: David Silverman
candidates.proposition: An omnipotent God could realize any later good without childhood cancer, so unknown future benefits do not reconcile suffering with benevolence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Silverman answers Turek's enumerated defense point by point and restates the challenge to omnipotence and benevolence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The rebuttal targets the central skeptical-theist response and argues that divine power makes severe suffering unnecessary even if later goods exist.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Turek's claim that finite humans cannot know whether present evil produces greater goods later in time or eternity.

candidates.contextSummary: Silverman rejects appeals to human limitation and an afterlife, arguing that an all-powerful being could secure every proposed benefit without leukemia or comparable evil.
